stories.title: DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.
stories.summary: Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PHvP Prefer DW on Google The average human brain consumes about 20% of the body's energy despite making up only around 2% of its weight. Interestingly, that stays roughly stable whether you are resting or busy with a complex task. Image: Irina Romanova/Zoonar/picture alliance Advertisement You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes. Your brain has its own version of that. Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift? Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing. It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas. That's your brain's default mode network. "Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression ," wrote the signatories of the appeal. The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English. stories.article_text_excerpt: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack By Sarah Rainsford Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent ,Â Reporting from Krakow Published 9 hours ago Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend. The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times. As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower. Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died. Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened. stories.article_text_excerpt: Cancer claims 10 million lives each year, the global shortage of health workers runs into the millions, and in some parts of the world, a single mosquito bite can be fatal. These challenges may seem very different. Yet they share a common element in how many health systems operate: risk is often recognised only after it has become illness, outbreak or crisis. By then, a disease may have advanced, transmission of disease may be under way, or an already stretched workforce may be managing consequences that earlier action could have reduced. The opportunity is to move that point of intervention earlier. This is what anticipatory health means in practice: using signals that already exist, at the bedside, in communities, and in routine health data, to help people and health systems act sooner. It is not prediction for its own sake. The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response. The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
